name: 3Sum
hints: Fix one number, then the rest becomes a Two Sum on a sorted array.
Sort first, then for each index use two pointers on the remainder to find pairs summing to its negative.
Skip over duplicate values at every pointer to avoid duplicate triplets.

name: Accounts Merge
hints: Accounts sharing any email should be merged into one — that's a Union-Find grouping problem.
Union all accounts that share at least one email, using the first-seen account for each email to detect overlaps.
After unioning, group emails by their root account and sort each group's emails before output.

name: Add Two Numbers
hints: Digits are stored in reverse order, so you can add from the least significant digit directly.
Track a carry value as you sum corresponding digits from both lists.
Don't forget a final extra node if a carry remains after both lists are exhausted.

name: Alien Dictionary
hints: Word order implies letter order — the first differing character between adjacent words gives you one ordering constraint.
Build a directed graph of "this letter comes before that letter," then topologically sort it.
Watch the edge case where a later word is a prefix of an earlier one — that's invalid and has no valid ordering.

name: Balanced Binary Tree
hints: Balanced means every node's two subtrees differ in height by at most 1.
A naive check recomputes height repeatedly — instead, have height-checking return -1 as an "unbalanced" signal.
Once any subtree reports unbalanced, short-circuit and propagate that -1 straight up without further checking.

name: Basic Calculator II
hints: Without parentheses, you just need to respect */ having higher precedence than +-.
Track a running stack of terms; for + and -, push the (signed) number; for * and /, combine with the top of the stack immediately.
Summing the stack at the end naturally applies correct operator precedence.

name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
hints: You only need one pass, tracking the minimum price seen so far.
At each day, the best possible profit is today's price minus the minimum-so-far.
Track a running max-profit as you go rather than storing every price.

name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
hints: After selling, you can't buy the very next day — that's the twist versus a plain buy/sell problem.
Track separate running states for holding a stock, just sold (in cooldown), and free to buy.
Each day, each state's new value depends only on yesterday's states — no need to store more than the previous day.

name: Binary Search
hints: Compare the middle element to the target and eliminate half the space each time.
Use left <= right as your loop condition to avoid missing the last element.
Watch for integer overflow when computing mid — use left + (right-left)/2.

name: Binary Search Tree Iterator
hints: You need next() and hasNext() in average O(1), which rules out a full precomputed in-order list for large trees.
Maintain a stack, pushing all left-children down to the leftmost node initially.
On next(), pop a node, and if it has a right child, push that child and all of its left descendants.

name: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
hints: You need to group nodes by level, so a plain DFS needs extra bookkeeping — BFS is more natural.
Use a queue, and process it one full level at a time by tracking the queue's size at the start of each level.
For each of those "size" nodes, dequeue it, record its value, and enqueue its children before moving to the next level.

name: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
hints: A path can start and end anywhere, and doesn't have to pass through the root.
At each node, the best path through it is node value plus the best of (left, 0) plus the best of (right, 0), clamping negative contributions to zero.
What you return upward to the parent is different — only node value plus the better single side, since a path can't branch through a node it's passing through.

name: Binary Tree Right Side View
hints: You want the last node visible at each level, looking from the right.
A level-order (BFS) traversal naturally lets you grab the last node processed at each level.
Alternatively, DFS right-before-left and record the first node seen at each new depth.

name: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
hints: The AND of a whole range only keeps bits that stay constant across every number in it.
Repeatedly right-shift both m and n together until they're equal — that shared prefix is the common bits.
Shift the result back left by however many shifts you performed to restore the original bit positions.

name: Allocate Minimum Pages
hints: If a maximum page load is feasible, any larger maximum is feasible too. Search that load between the largest book and the total number of pages.
For a proposed limit, scan books in order, assigning contiguous books to one student until the next would exceed the limit, then start another student.
A limit is feasible if the scan uses at most the available students; reject more students than books when each must receive a book. Keep the smallest feasible limit and use wide totals.

name: Burst Balloons
hints: Think about which balloon you burst LAST in a given range, not first — that reframes it into clean subproblems.
dp[i][j] is the best score for bursting all balloons strictly between i and j, given i and j survive as boundaries.
Try every possible last-balloon-burst k inside (i, j), and combine dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + the product of the three boundary values.

name: Candy
hints: Every child must get at least one candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbor needs more candy than that neighbor.
Do two passes: left to right, bump a candy count whenever the current rating beats the previous; right to left, do the same in reverse.
Combine both passes by taking the max of the two computed values at each position.

name: Car Fleet
hints: Sort by starting position — only the car closest to the destination can "lead" a fleet.
Compute each car's arrival time if it never had to slow down.
Process from closest-to-destination backward; a car merges into the fleet ahead if its time is at most the fleet leader's.

name: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
hints: Plain Dijkstra doesn't account for the "at most K stops" limit directly.
Bellman-Ford, relaxing edges for at most K+1 rounds, naturally respects the stop limit.
Use the previous round's costs (not values already updated this round) so you don't chain more than one extra stop per round.

name: Climbing Stairs
hints: To reach step n, you came from either step n-1 or step n-2.
That means ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) — this is just Fibonacci in disguise.
You only need the last two values at any point, so you can solve it in O(1) space.

name: Clone Graph
hints: You need to recreate every node and every edge without infinite-looping on cycles.
A hash map from original node to cloned node lets you detect "already cloned" and avoid revisiting.
Clone a node the first time you see it, then recurse into its neighbors, wiring up clones via the map.
A prime has exactly two positive divisors. Reject values below two, then look for a divisor rather than trying to construct prime numbers.
Test candidate divisors only through the square root. If a larger factor exists, its paired smaller factor must already have been encountered.
Handle two separately and skip larger even divisors after rejecting even inputs. Use divisor <= number / divisor if squaring the divisor might overflow, and follow CodeChef's required output wording.
name: Primality Test
Coin Change
hints: This is bottom-up: figure out the min coins for every amount from 0 up to the target.
minCoins(amount) = 1 + the minimum over every coin at most amount of minCoins(amount - coin).
Initialize impossible amounts to infinity, and if the target amount is still infinity at the end, return -1.

name: Coin Change II
hints: Unlike Coin Change (min coins), here you're counting the number of distinct combinations that sum to the target.
Process one coin type at a time, updating reachable-amount counts, so order doesn't create duplicate combinations.
Iterate amounts upward (not downward) per coin, since reusing the same coin multiple times is allowed here.

name: Combination Sum
hints: The same number can be reused, so your recursion should allow revisiting the current index.
At each step, either include the current candidate again or move to the next candidate.
Sort first so you can break early once the remaining target goes negative.

name: Combination Sum II
hints: Unlike Combination Sum, each number can only be used once here.
Sort first, then advance the index by one each recursive call instead of allowing reuse.
Use the same skip-identical-siblings trick as Subsets II to avoid duplicate combinations.

name: Combinations
hints: You're choosing k elements out of n where order doesn't matter.
Recurse with a start index, only ever moving forward, to avoid generating the same combination twice.
Prune early once the remaining elements available can't possibly fill out the combination to size k.

name: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
hints: Preorder's first element is always the current subtree's root.
Find that root's position in the inorder slice — everything left of it is the left subtree, everything right is the right subtree.
A hash map from value to inorder index turns that lookup into O(1) instead of a scan.

name: Container With Most Water
hints: The brute-force pair check is O(n^2) — two pointers gets you to O(n).
Start at both ends; area is limited by the shorter line, so move that pointer inward.
Moving the taller line inward can only ever decrease or keep the width-limited area, never help.

name: Contains Duplicate
hints: Think about what data structure gives O(1) membership checks.
A set lets you check "have I seen this before" in one pass.
If the set's final size is smaller than the array, a duplicate exists.

name: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
hints: A height-balanced BST from sorted data naturally picks the middle element as the root.
Recursively pick the middle of each subarray range as that subtree's root.
Recurse on the left half for the left subtree and the right half for the right subtree.

name: Copy List with Random Pointer
hints: The tricky part is the random pointer, which can point anywhere, including forward.
A hash map from original node to cloned node lets you look up any random target instantly.
Do it in two passes: first create all clone nodes, then wire up next and random using the map.

name: Count Digits in a Number
hints: Removing the final decimal digit is integer division by ten. Repeating that operation counts how many positions the representation contains.
Count each division until the number becomes zero, but return one immediately when the original input is zero.
Avoid floating-point logarithms for this basic task because powers of ten and zero need careful treatment. Work on a copy if the original input must remain available.

name: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
hints: A node is "good" if no ancestor on its path from the root has a greater value.
Pass the maximum value seen so far down the recursion as you descend.
At each node, compare it to that running max — if it's at least as big, count it and update the max for its children.

name: Subarray Sum Equals K
hints: A subarray sum is the difference between two prefix sums. At the current prefix, count how many earlier prefixes equal currentSum minus the target.
Initialize the frequency of prefix sum zero to one so intervals beginning at index zero are included. Query before inserting the current prefix to avoid counting an empty interval.
Store frequencies rather than one index because several earlier prefixes can contribute different subarrays. This works with negative values, unlike a positivity-based sliding window.

name: Counting Bits
hints: You can reuse previously computed answers instead of recounting bits from scratch for every number.
The bit count of i equals the bit count of (i with its lowest set bit removed), plus 1.
i AND (i-1) is that "lowest set bit removed" value, and it's always smaller than i, so it's already computed.

name: Course Schedule
hints: This is really "does this dependency graph contain a cycle?"
Track each course's in-degree (prerequisite count) and process courses with zero remaining prerequisites first.
If you can process every course this way (Kahn's algorithm), there's no cycle; if some remain stuck, a cycle exists.

name: Course Schedule II
hints: Same cycle-detection idea as Course Schedule, but now you also need the valid order itself.
Kahn's algorithm naturally produces a valid order as a side effect of processing zero-in-degree nodes.
If the resulting order doesn't include every course, a cycle exists — return an empty array.

name: Weird Algorithm
hints: Simulate Collatz sequence until 1.

name: Repetitions
hints: Track longest contiguous equal characters.

name: Permutation
hints: Handle small n separately, then print evens then odds.

name: Missing Number
hints: Use sum formula or xor to find missing value.

name: Apartments
hints: Two pointers over sorted applicants and apartments.

name: Ferris Wheel
hints: Pair lightest with heaviest greedily.

name: Concert Tickets
hints: Multiset / tree map predecessor query per customer.

name: Increasing Array
hints: Greedily raise each element to previous max.

name: Book Shop
hints: Choose each book at most once while maximizing pages within the price budget. This is a 0/1 knapsack model, not fractional selection.
Let best[budget] store the most pages obtainable from processed books. For each book, update budgets downward using its price and page count so the same book cannot be reused.
Initialize all budgets to zero because selecting no books is allowed. Ignore books costing more than the budget; the one-dimensional table uses O(budget) memory and O(books * budget) time.

name: Counting Rooms
hints: Count connected components in grid using DFS/BFS.

name: Labyrinth
hints: BFS shortest path and parent reconstruction.

name: Restaurant Customers
hints: Sweep line with sorted arrivals/departures.

name: Distinct Numbers
hints: Count unique using set after reading all values.

name: Dice Combinations
hints: dp[x] = sum(dp[x-1..x-6]).

name: Minimizing Coins
hints: Classic min-coin unbounded knapsack DP.

name: Coin Combinations I
hints: Count ordered ways using DP by sum.
The array never changes, so a preprocessing pass can answer many interval-sum queries without rescanning their elements.
Build a prefix array with an initial zero. The sum of the judge's one-based inclusive range from left to right is prefix[right] - prefix[left - 1].
Use a wide integer type for totals because many large array values may be added. Preprocessing is O(n), each query is O(1), and no tree structure is necessary for the immutable case.
name: Static Range Sum Queries

hints: A point change affects many ordinary prefix totals. A Fenwick tree stores overlapping binary-sized blocks so each update and prefix query touches only logarithmically many entries.
Use one-based indices. Add a delta along index += index & -index; read a prefix along index -= index & -index, accumulating the stored block totals.

Type 1 assigns a new value rather than adding it, so update by newValue minus the saved old value. Type 2 answers prefix[right] - prefix[left - 1]; keep both stored values and sums in wide integer types.
name: Dynamic Range Sum Queries

hints: Unlike sums, interval minima cannot be obtained by subtracting two prefix minima. Store a mergeable minimum for a hierarchy of array intervals.
Build a segment tree whose parent stores the minimum of its children. A point assignment changes one leaf and the ancestors on its path to the root.

Answer a range by combining only fully covered tree intervals, using positive infinity for disjoint pieces. Convert the judge's one-based inclusive endpoints consistently; both updates and queries take O(log n).
name: Dynamic Range Minimum Queries
Message Route
hints: Unweighted shortest path via BFS.

name: Building Teams
hints: Check bipartite coloring with BFS/DFS.

name: Shortest Routes I
hints: Dijkstra from source over adjacency list.

name: Array Description
hints: DP by index and value with neighbor transitions.

name: Daily Temperatures
hints: For each day you need the next day with a higher temperature — a stack tracks "waiting" days.
Keep a monotonically decreasing stack of indices (temperatures decreasing top to bottom).
When a warmer day appears, pop and resolve every colder day still on the stack in one pass.

name: Decode Ways
hints: Each position can potentially be decoded alone, or paired with the next digit — but not always.
ways(i) = ways(i-1) if digit i is valid alone, plus ways(i-2) if digits i-1 and i form a valid 10-26 pair.
A zero can never stand alone — it's only valid as the second digit of a 10 or 20 pair.

name: Building H2O
hints: Each group needs exactly two hydrogen threads and one oxygen thread. Represent those permits separately.
Use a barrier or equivalent phase state so the next molecule cannot release atoms before the current group finishes.
Waiting threads should block on synchronization primitives rather than relying on scheduling order or timed sleeps.

name: Design a Food Rating System
hints: Keep food metadata by name and a separate ranking index for each cuisine.
Rank by descending rating and then ascending food name; ties are part of the contract.
Updating a rating must invalidate its old ranking entry. An ordered set or a heap with stale-entry checks can support this.

name: Design a Text Editor
hints: Represent text on the two sides of the cursor separately so edits do not repeatedly copy the whole document.
Two stacks let cursor movement transfer characters between sides while insertion and deletion operate at the left boundary.
Clamp movement and deletion to available characters, and return only the required final ten characters to the cursor's left.

name: Design Authentication Manager
hints: Store each token's expiration time rather than repeatedly computing its age from creation.
A token expiring at the current timestamp is already invalid and cannot be renewed.
Keep generation, renewal, and counting consistent about expiration; the judge's operation limit determines whether scanning is sufficient.

name: Design Browser History
hints: Track both the current position and the end of valid history; they are different after moving backward.
Visiting a new URL discards the forward branch instead of appending to the old future.
Clamp back and forward operations to the valid bounds, including requests larger than the stored history.

name: Design Circular Queue
hints: A fixed array, a head index, and a size counter are enough to distinguish full from empty without shifting elements.
Compute insertion and rear positions modulo capacity, taking special care when the queue is empty.
Failed enqueue or dequeue operations must leave every index and the size unchanged.

name: Design HashMap
hints: Implement the storage yourself rather than wrapping the language's built-in hash map.
Separate bucket selection from collision handling, and update an existing key instead of inserting a second copy.
Use the key-range constraints to compare direct addressing with bucketed storage; preserve the required missing-key sentinel.

name: Design a Hit Counter - Multi-Threaded
hints: Store an independent counter per page and initialize every page to zero when init is called.
Concurrent increments to the same page must be atomic; consider per-page synchronization or atomic counters instead of a global bottleneck.
The Java judge is multithreaded; Python is single-threaded. Counts are cumulative, with no sliding time window or expiry.

name: Design Movie Rental System
hints: Identify each copy by its shop and movie IDs, with separate indexes for available copies and all rented copies.
Search orders available copies by price then shop; reports also need the movie ID as a tie breaker.
Rent and drop must move the same copy between indexes atomically so queries never report stale availability.

name: Design Parking System
hints: This exercise tracks capacity for three car sizes; it does not ask for tickets, floors, or parking fees.
Encapsulate the remaining capacity by car type and validate availability before decrementing it.
A rejected car must not change capacity, including when a category starts with zero spaces.

name: Design Underground System
hints: Keep active check-ins keyed by passenger separately from completed-trip statistics keyed by ordered station pairs.
A route only needs total travel time and trip count to answer average queries; storing every completed trip is unnecessary.
Remove the active check-in after checkout and keep opposite directions as distinct routes.

name: My Calendar I
hints: Bookings are half-open intervals: an event ending exactly when another starts is allowed.
Two intervals overlap only when each one's start is strictly before the other's end.
Check conflicts before inserting. With an ordered structure, the nearest earlier and later bookings are enough.

name: My Calendar II
hints: Track accepted bookings and the intervals already covered twice.
Reject a new event if it intersects any double-booked interval; otherwise its overlaps with existing events become new double bookings.
Do not leave partial overlap records after a rejected request. Half-open boundaries apply here too.

name: Print FooBar Alternately
hints: Treat alternation as handing a permit from one thread to the other.
Initially only foo may print; after printing, each thread releases the other thread's permit.
Do not rely on thread start order or sleeps. The required sequence must hold under arbitrary scheduling.

name: Print in Order
hints: The dependency is completion of the first callback before the second, and completion of the second before the third.
Two one-shot synchronization signals can encode those dependencies regardless of thread start order.
Signal completion after invoking the callback, not merely after entering its method.

name: Print Zero Even Odd
hints: Model whose turn it is explicitly: zero, odd, or even.
After zero prints, release the number thread matching the next value's parity; that thread returns control to zero.
Check the final iteration so no thread waits for a signal that will never be sent.

name: Seat Reservation Manager
hints: The API always reserves the smallest available seat, so a queue in insertion order is insufficient.
Use a min-heap for returned seats and a counter for seats that have never been reserved.
Keep reservation and unreservation as inverse state changes without inserting a seat into the available pool twice.

name: Simple Bank System
hints: Convert the API's one-based account numbers carefully and validate both accounts before a transfer.
A transfer is one operation: check funds and validity before changing either balance.
Use a numeric type large enough for the constraints, and keep failed withdrawals or transfers free of side effects.

name: Snapshot Array
hints: Store a versioned history per array index instead of copying the entire array for every snapshot.
Multiple writes at the same snapshot ID can replace the last history entry for that index.
A lookup needs the latest recorded version at or before the requested snapshot; binary search that boundary.

name: The Dining Philosophers
hints: Acquiring the left fork first in every thread creates a circular wait; break that cycle deliberately.
A global fork acquisition order or a limit on simultaneous contenders can prevent deadlock.
Protect each fork's ownership and pair every acquisition with a release, keeping callbacks within the correct ownership interval.

name: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
hints: This is a trie, plus a wildcard character that can match any letter.
On a normal character, descend into exactly one child; on the wildcard, you must try every child.
That wildcard case means search needs to be recursive (or use a stack) to explore multiple branches.

name: Design an ATM Machine
hints: Track counts for the five supported denominations; this judge covers deposits and withdrawals, not card or PIN sessions.
Withdraw greedily from the largest denomination exactly as specified. Do not search for a different combination when that policy fails.
Compute a proposed withdrawal against temporary counts, then commit only when the entire amount can be dispensed.

name: Design Amazon (E-commerce Marketplace)
hints: Keep catalog discovery separate from authoritative inventory and checkout.
Use durable reservations, idempotent payment attempts, and an order state machine with compensations.

name: Design Analytics Event Pipeline
hints: Ingestion, durable queue, stream processing, and warehouse sink.
Handle backpressure, schema evolution, and replays.

name: Design API Gateway
hints: Responsibilities: auth, throttling, routing, observability.
Discuss plugin chain and resilience under dependency failures.

name: Design Distributed Cache
hints: Sharding via consistent hashing with replication.
Cover invalidation, TTL policies, and hot-key mitigation.

name: Design Food Delivery Platform
hints: Order orchestration and dispatch assignment loop.
Estimate ETAs with dynamic traffic-aware updates.

name: Design LFU Cache
hints: Eviction needs least-frequently-used, ties broken by least-recently-used.
Track per-key frequency, and group keys by frequency using an ordered structure (frequency → doubly linked list of keys).
Track the current minimum frequency so eviction always checks the right bucket in O(1).

name: Design LRU Cache
hints: Needs O(1) get/put — combine a hash map (key → node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency.
Core classes: Cache, Node (key, value, prev, next). Move a node to the front on every access.
Evict from the tail when capacity is exceeded; watch for the head/tail sentinel-node edge cases.

name: Design Netflix (Video on Demand)
hints: Separate entitlement and playback-session APIs from the CDN media path.
Publish immutable renditions only after validation; measure startup time and rebuffering by device and network.

name: Design BookMyShow (Ticket Booking)
hints: Keep seat ownership authoritative per show, with atomic all-or-none holds for a requested seat group.
Fence expired holds and reconcile delayed payments instead of allowing a stale callback to sell a seat twice.

name: Design Instagram (Photo Sharing)
hints: Separate media ingestion and moderation from feed fan-out and read-time authorization.
Treat timeline entries as disposable references; privacy changes and deletions must still be enforced when serving media.

name: Design Google Drive / Dropbox
hints: Upload immutable bytes separately from transactional file metadata and permission changes.
Use version preconditions and a durable change cursor to preserve conflicting offline edits and recover missed notifications.

name: Design Twitter / X (News Feed)
hints: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read trade-off.
Use caching and ranking for personalized timelines.

name: Design Notification System
hints: Multi-channel delivery (push/email/SMS) with retry queues.
Handle idempotency and per-user preferences.

name: Design Payment System
hints: Ledger consistency and idempotent transaction APIs.
Reconciliation, fraud checks, and failure recovery are critical.

name: Design Pub/Sub Messaging Platform
hints: Partition topics and manage consumer offsets.
Guarantee trade-offs: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once.

name: Design Rate Limiter at Scale
hints: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, and sliding window counters.
Discuss distributed counters, consistency, and fallback behavior.

name: Design WhatsApp (Messaging)
hints: Persistent connections (WebSocket), message fan-out, and presence.
Storage split: hot recent messages vs archival history.

name: Design Recommendation System
hints: Blend candidate generation and ranking stages.
Discuss feature freshness and model serving constraints.

name: Design Uber (Ride Sharing)
hints: Location indexing and driver-rider matching strategy.
Handle surge pricing and trip state transitions.

name: Design Search Autocomplete
hints: Offline indexing pipeline plus low-latency serving tier.
Ranking signals and typo tolerance are key differentiators.

name: Design Twitter
hints: You need the 10 most recent tweets across everyone a user follows, merged and ordered by time.
Track a global increasing timestamp/counter alongside each tweet.
Use a heap to merge each followed user's most recent tweets efficiently rather than sorting everything.

name: Design URL Shortener
hints: Define read/write ratio, key generation, and redirect latency goals.
Core pieces: API, key-value store, cache, analytics pipeline.

name: Design YouTube (Video Sharing)
hints: Upload/transcoding pipeline and CDN delivery.
Store metadata, watch history, and recommendation hooks.

name: Detect Squares
hints: For every added point, you need fast lookups of "how many points exist at a given coordinate."
A hash map counting occurrences of each (x, y) point gives O(1) existence/count checks.
For a query point, try every existing point sharing its x-coordinate as one diagonal corner, then check if the other two required corners exist too.

name: Diagonal Traverse
hints: Cells on the same diagonal share the same (row + col) value.
Group cells by that diagonal index, then alternate the read direction between consecutive diagonals.
Careful boundary handling at the matrix edges determines the exact start/end of each diagonal.

name: Diameter of Binary Tree
hints: The diameter is a path length, and it doesn't have to pass through the root.
At every node, the longest path through it is left-depth plus right-depth.
Track a running max of that sum while a helper function returns depth upward, so you only traverse once.

name: Dijkstra Algorithm
hints: Breadth-first layers work only for equal edge costs. With nonnegative weights, expand the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance instead.
Initialize the source distance to zero and use a min-heap of distance-vertex pairs. Relax an edge only when the candidate distance improves the neighbor's best known distance.

Skip a popped pair if its distance differs from the current best value. Do not mark vertices finished when first inserted; a cheaper route may still arrive. Negative edges require a different shortest-path algorithm.

name: Distinct Subsequences
hints: You're counting ways to pick characters from s (keeping order) to spell out t exactly.
dp[i][j] is the number of ways using the first i characters of s to form the first j characters of t.
If s[i] matches t[j], you can either use it or skip it — add both possibilities; if it doesn't match, you can only skip it in s.

name: Edit Distance
hints: At each pair of positions, you're choosing the cheapest of insert, delete, or replace.
If the current characters match, no edit's needed — carry forward the diagonal value unchanged.
Otherwise take 1 plus the minimum of the three neighboring cells (insert, delete, replace).

name: Encode and Decode Strings
hints: You can't just join with a delimiter — the delimiter itself might appear in a string.
Prefix each string with its length so decoding always knows exactly where it ends.
Use a fixed separator right after the length (e.g. 5#hello) so parsing is unambiguous.

name: Evaluate Division
hints: Each equation a/b = k defines a weighted, directed edge in both directions (b/a = 1/k).
Build a graph of variables connected by ratio-weighted edges, then DFS/BFS multiplying edge weights along the path.
A query where either variable never appeared in any equation has no valid path, so the answer is -1.0.

name: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
hints: Postfix notation means operators come after their operands — a stack processes this naturally.
Push numbers; on an operator, pop two, apply it, and push the result back.
Watch operand order for subtraction and division — the second-popped value comes first.

name: Excel Sheet Column Number
hints: This is base-26 conversion, but with digits 1-26 instead of 0-25.
Process characters left to right, multiplying the running total by 26 and adding the current letter's value (A=1).
No special zero-digit handling is needed since there's no "0" in this numbering system.

name: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
hints: Generating all pairs and sorting is wasteful when both arrays are already sorted.
Start with pairs (0, j) in a min-heap keyed by sum, one per starting index in the second array (up to k).
Popping the smallest and pushing its "next in the first array" neighbor keeps the heap small while still exploring in sum order.

name: Find Median from Data Stream
hints: Sorting on every insert is too slow — you want the middle without a full sort.
Keep two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half of numbers, a min-heap for the larger half.
Keep the heaps balanced in size (differing by at most 1); the median comes from the top(s) of the heaps.

name: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
hints: The array is sorted then rotated — one half is always properly ordered.
Compare the middle to the rightmost element to decide which half contains the rotation point.
If mid's value is greater than right's value, the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it's at or before mid.

name: Find the Duplicate Number
hints: You can't modify the array or use extra space, which rules out sorting or a set.
Treat each value as a "next pointer" (index to arr[index]) — a duplicate creates a cycle.
Floyd's cycle detection (same idea as Linked List Cycle) finds the duplicate as the cycle's entry point.

name: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
hints: A direct comparison from every starting position is a useful baseline, but repeated pattern prefixes cause the same text characters to be compared many times.
Build KMP's prefix table: for each pattern prefix, store the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On mismatch, follow that table until a compatible shorter prefix remains.

Scan the text without moving its pointer backward, updating the matched pattern length through the prefix table. A full match ends at the current text index, so subtract patternLength - 1 to return its starting position.

name: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
hints: The final structure follows preorder traversal order, using only right pointers.
Process nodes in reverse preorder (right, left, root), keeping a "previously processed" pointer.
Set the current node's right to the previous node and left to null, then update previous to the current node.

name: Frog Jump
hints: The final jump to a step must come from one or two positions earlier. Its cost is the absolute difference between the two endpoint heights.
Store the minimum total energy to reach each step. Take the smaller of the valid predecessor totals plus their respective jump costs.
The first step costs zero, and the second has only one predecessor. Only the last two totals are needed for a constant-extra-space version after the recurrence is correct.

name: Game of Life
hints: Every cell's next state depends on the current state of its 8 neighbors — updating in place risks reading already-updated cells.
Encode both the old and new state in each cell using extra bits (e.g. 2 = was-dead-now-alive), then decode in a second pass.
Count live neighbors before deciding a cell's next state, using only the low bit (original state) during counting.

name: Gas Station
hints: If the total gas is less than the total cost, no valid starting station exists at all.
Track a running tank total; whenever it goes negative, no station before this point could have been a valid start either.
The station right after the last point the tank went negative is the unique valid starting point (when a solution exists).

name: Generate Parentheses
hints: This is backtracking, not a formula — build strings and prune invalid branches.
Track counts of open and close brackets used so far.
You can add a close bracket only if close count is less than open count, and an open bracket only if open count is less than n.

name: Graph Valid Tree
hints: A valid tree needs exactly n-1 edges and full connectivity — check both.
If the edge count isn't exactly n-1, you can return false immediately without further checks.
Otherwise, Union-Find (or a single DFS/BFS) confirms whether all nodes end up in one connected group.

name: Group Anagrams
hints: Anagrams share the same letters, just reordered.
A sorted version of each word makes a great group key.
Map that sorted-string key to a list of original words in a hash map.

name: Hand of Straights
hints: You need to form consecutive-value groups of a fixed size from the whole hand.
Count occurrences of each card, then always try to build a group starting from the smallest remaining card.
If any of the groupSize consecutive cards needed is unavailable, the hand can't be rearranged — return false.

name: Happy Number
hints: Repeatedly summing squared digits either reaches 1, or falls into a repeating cycle that never reaches 1.
This is a cycle-detection problem — Floyd's slow/fast pointer trick applies directly to the sequence of values.
Alternatively, a hash set of seen values lets you detect a repeat (and therefore an infinite non-1 cycle) directly.

name: House Robber
hints: You can't rob two adjacent houses — decide, at each house, to include it or skip it.
best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + value[i]) — either skip this house or take it plus the best two houses back.
Only the previous two computed values are ever needed, so this reduces to O(1) space.

name: House Robber II
hints: The houses are in a circle now, so the first and last house can't both be robbed.
Run the regular House Robber logic twice: once excluding the last house, once excluding the first.
The answer is the max of those two runs — this sidesteps the circular constraint entirely.

name: Implement Queue using Stacks
hints: A queue is FIFO but a stack is LIFO — you need two stacks to flip the order back.
Push new elements onto an "in" stack; when the "out" stack is empty, dump everything from "in" into "out" to reverse the order.
Only transfer between stacks when "out" is empty, keeping the amortized cost O(1) per operation.

name: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
hints: Each node needs children (one per possible character) and a flag marking "a word ends here."
Insert by walking/creating a child node per character, then marking the last node as end-of-word.
search() and startsWith() are nearly identical — the only difference is checking that end-of-word flag at the end.

name: Infix to Postfix
hints: Operands can go directly to the output. Operators must wait until every operand in their higher-priority subexpression has been emitted.
Keep operators and opening parentheses on a stack. A closing parenthesis flushes operators until its matching opener; do not emit either parenthesis.

Pop higher-precedence operators before pushing a new one. Pop equal precedence only for left-associative operators: exponentiation is right-associative, so a^b^c becomes abc^^. Flush remaining operators at the end.

name: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
hints: Random access in O(1) suggests an array; O(1) delete-by-value suggests a hash map.
Combine both: a hash map from value to its index in a backing array.
To delete in O(1), swap the target with the array's last element before popping, updating the map for the swapped element.

name: Insert Interval
hints: The existing intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, which you can take advantage of.
Add every interval that ends before the new one starts, untouched.
Merge all intervals that overlap the new one into a single combined interval, then add every interval that starts after it ends.

name: Integer to Roman
hints: Roman numerals are built greedily from the largest values down.
Keep a sorted list of (value, symbol) pairs including subtractive combinations like (900, "CM").
Repeatedly subtract the largest value that fits and append its symbol, moving to smaller values as needed.

name: Interleaving String
hints: Track how much of each of the two source strings you've consumed to build a prefix of the result.
dp[i][j] is true if the first i characters of s1 and first j characters of s2 can interleave into the first i+j characters of s3.
At each cell, check whether the next needed character can come validly from s1's next character, from s2's next character, or neither.

name: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
hints: The two lists might have different lengths before they converge.
Walk two pointers, one per list; when a pointer reaches its list's end, redirect it to the other list's head.
Both pointers travel the same total distance this way, so they meet exactly at the intersection (or both hit null together).

name: Invert Binary Tree
hints: "Invert" means swap every node's left and right children.
A simple recursive swap at every node, then recurse into both (now-swapped) children, solves it.
This also works iteratively with a queue or stack instead of recursion.

name: Is Graph Bipartite?
hints: A graph is bipartite if you can 2-color it so no edge connects same-colored nodes.
BFS or DFS from each uncolored component, coloring neighbors the opposite color of the current node.
If you ever find a neighbor already colored the same as the current node, it's not bipartite.

name: Jump Game
hints: You don't need to know every path — just whether the farthest reachable index ever covers the end.
Track the farthest index reachable so far as you scan left to right.
If you ever reach an index beyond your current farthest-reachable point, you're stuck — return false immediately.

name: Jump Game II
hints: You want the minimum number of jumps, not just whether reaching the end is possible.
Track the current jump's reachable boundary and the farthest boundary reachable with one more jump.
Increment the jump count exactly when you reach the current boundary, then advance both boundaries.

name: K Closest Points to Origin
hints: You don't need to fully sort all points, just find the closest k.
A max-heap of size k (by distance) lets you discard the farthest point whenever the heap overflows.
Compare squared distances to avoid unnecessary square-root calls.

name: Koko Eating Bananas
hints: You're not searching the array — you're searching over possible "eating speeds."
For a given speed, you can compute the total hours needed in one pass.
Binary search the speed: if hours needed is at most h, try slower; otherwise go faster.

name: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
hints: You need the kth largest after every addition, not just once.
A min-heap of size k always has the kth largest sitting at its top.
On each add, push the value and pop the smallest if the heap exceeds size k. GFG expects -1 for prefixes with fewer than k values; once k values exist, report the heap root.

name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
hints: You only need the k largest values seen so far. Of those retained candidates, the smallest is the first one a better arrival should replace.
Use a min-heap: push each value and remove the root whenever the size exceeds k. Keep duplicate values; this is kth largest, not kth distinct.
After the scan, the root is the kth largest. This uses O(n log k) time and O(k) space; quickselect is an alternative when streaming updates are not needed.

name: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
hints: An in-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted order.
Do an in-order traversal and just count nodes as you go.
You can stop as soon as you hit the kth node — no need to traverse the whole tree.

name: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
hints: For each bar, find the widest interval in which no bar is shorter. Its height can support a rectangle throughout that interval.
Compute NSL and NSR as indices with increasing stacks. Pop greater or equal heights in both passes; use -1 and the array length when a boundary is missing.
For each index, area = height * (rightSmaller - leftSmaller - 1). Equal-height bars may share the same full width. Take the maximum using a sufficiently wide numeric type.

name: Largest subarray with 0 sum
hints: Two equal prefix sums enclose a subarray summing to zero. To maximize its length, retain the earliest occurrence of each sum.
Seed prefix sum zero at index -1. At each position, compare the current index with the stored earliest index for the current prefix sum.
Do not overwrite an earlier occurrence with a later one. Distinguish this map of earliest positions from the frequency map used to count all subarrays of a given sum.

name: Last Stone Weight
hints: You always need the two current heaviest stones — a max-heap gives you that instantly.
Pop the top two, and if they differ, push the difference back in.
A min-heap can simulate a max-heap by pushing negated values.

name: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
hints: Each digit maps to a fixed set of letters — this is a Cartesian product built one digit at a time.
Recurse digit by digit, appending one of that digit's letters to the current path each time.
An empty input should return an empty list, not a list containing an empty string — handle that edge case.

name: LFU Cache
hints: You need O(1) get/put while evicting the least-frequently-used (ties broken by least-recently-used).
Track each key's frequency, and group keys by frequency using an ordered structure (e.g. per-frequency doubly linked lists).
Track the current minimum frequency so eviction always checks the right frequency bucket first.

name: Linked List Cycle
hints: You need O(1) space, so a visited-set isn't the intended solution.
Use two pointers moving at different speeds — one step and two steps at a time.
If there's a cycle, the faster pointer will eventually lap and equal the slower one.

name: Longest Common Subsequence
hints: Compare characters of both strings position by position, building a 2D table of best-so-far lengths.
If the current characters match, extend the diagonal value by 1; otherwise take the max of the cell above or to the left.
Use an extra row and column of zeros as padding so you don't need special-case logic at the string boundaries.

name: Longest Consecutive Sequence
hints: Sorting works but the O(n) approach avoids it entirely — think hash set.
Put every number in a set, then only start counting a sequence from numbers whose (num-1) isn't in the set.
That check guarantees each full sequence is only ever counted once, from its start.

name: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
hints: From every cell, the longest increasing path is 1 plus the best result from any strictly-greater neighbor.
Plain DFS recomputes the same cells repeatedly — cache each cell's answer once computed (memoization).
Because values only increase along a path, there are no cycles to worry about, so memoized DFS is safe.

name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
hints: The O(n^2) version compares every pair — there's an O(n log n) version using binary search.
Maintain a list representing the smallest possible tail for an increasing subsequence of each length.
For each new number, binary search that list for where it belongs and replace there (or append if it's the largest so far).

name: Longest Palindromic Substring
hints: Every palindrome has a center — either a single character or between two characters.
Try expanding outward from every possible center, growing while both sides still match.
There are 2n-1 centers total — check them all and track the longest expansion.

name: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
hints: You're allowed k replacements — think window where (length - count of most frequent char) is at most k.
Track character counts in the current window and the count of its most frequent character.
The window never needs to shrink below its best-so-far size — only slide, don't shrink unnecessarily.

name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
hints: Expand a window to the right; when a repeat shows up, shrink from the left.
A hash set (or map of char to last index) tells you instantly if the new character is already in the window.
With a map of last-seen index, you can jump the left pointer directly past the repeat instead of shrinking step by step.

name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
hints: A BST's ordering tells you which direction to go without checking both subtrees.
If both target values are less than the current node, go left; if both are greater, go right.
The moment the two values split (one at or below current, one at or above), that current node is the answer.

name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
hints: Search both subtrees and return a found target or an already identified ancestor. A target node can itself be the ancestor of the other target.
Return immediately at null or either target. If the left and right recursive calls both return a node, the current node is where the two target paths join.

If only one child returns a node, propagate that result upward. Use reference identity and rely on the judge's guarantee that both targets exist; a missing-target variant requires additional presence tracking.

name: LRU Cache
hints: You need O(1) get and put, so no scanning to find the least-recently-used item.
Combine a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency.
On every get or put, move that node to the front; evict from the back when over capacity.

name: Majority Element
hints: The majority element appears more than n/2 times — think about a running "candidate" and a counter.
Boyer-Moore voting: increment the counter on a match with the candidate, decrement otherwise, swap candidate when the counter hits 0.
Because the majority element is guaranteed to exist, no verification pass is required.

name: Max Area of Island
hints: Very similar to Number of Islands, but now you need each island's size, not just the count.
Have your DFS/BFS return the count of cells visited during that flood-fill.
Track a running max across every island's returned size.

name: Maximal Square
hints: The largest square ending at a cell depends on three neighboring cells, not just one.
dp[i][j] (side length of the largest square with bottom-right corner at (i,j)) is 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]), if the cell itself is a 1.
Track a running max of dp values — the answer is that max, squared.

name: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
hints: The depth of a tree is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees.
Recurse on left and right, take the max, and add 1 for the current node.
A null node has depth 0 — that's your base case.

name: Maximum Product Subarray
hints: A single negative number can flip a very small product into the largest one — track both running max and running min.
At each element, the new max is the largest of (element alone, element times old max, element times old min).
Update both max and min together each step, since a min can become a max instantly if the next number's negative.

name: Maximum Subarray
hints: If your running sum ever goes negative, it can never help a future subarray — you're better off restarting from zero.
Keep a running sum, resetting it to 0 whenever it dips below zero, and track the max sum seen.
This is Kadane's algorithm — a single pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

name: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
hints: Merging both arrays is O(m+n) — the log-time approach binary searches a partition point.
Binary search a partition in the smaller array; the partition in the other array is then determined.
A valid partition has every left-side element at most every right-side element across both arrays.

name: Meeting Rooms
hints: This just asks whether ANY two meetings overlap.
Sort by start time, then check each meeting's start against the previous meeting's end.
Any start time earlier than the previous meeting's end time means overlap exists.

name: Meeting Rooms II
hints: You need the max number of meetings happening simultaneously at any point, not just whether any overlap.
Separately sort all start times and all end times, then walk through them together.
Each start increments a room counter, each end (when it comes before or with the next start) decrements it — track the running max.

name: Meeting Rooms II
hints: Min-heap of end times for active meetings.

name: Merge Intervals
hints: Sort by start time first — overlaps can only happen between intervals that are now adjacent.
Walk through sorted intervals, merging into the last added result whenever the current one's start is at or before that result's end.
When merging, update the result's end to the max of the two ends being merged, not just the new interval's end.

name: Merge k Sorted Lists
hints: Merging two at a time repeatedly works, but a heap gets you a cleaner O(n log k).
Push the head of every list into a min-heap keyed by value.
Pop the smallest, append it to the result, then push its next node (if any) back into the heap.

name: Merge Sorted Array
hints: Merging from the front requires shifting elements — merge from the back instead.
Compare the tail elements of both arrays and place the larger one at the very end of nums1.
If nums2 still has leftover elements when nums1's original elements are exhausted, copy them over directly.

name: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
hints: A triplet is only useful if none of its values exceed the corresponding target value.
Filter out any triplet where any coordinate overshoots the target's corresponding coordinate.
Among the remaining valid triplets, check if each target coordinate is matched by at least one of them.

name: Merge Two Sorted Lists
hints: This is like the merge step of merge sort, but on linked lists.
Use a dummy head node so you don't need special-case logic for the first node.
At each step, attach the smaller of the two current nodes and advance only that list.

name: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
hints: Similar recurrence to Climbing Stairs, but now each step choice has an associated cost.
cost-to-reach(i) = cost[i] + the smaller of cost-to-reach(i-1) and cost-to-reach(i-2).
You can start from either step 0 or step 1 for free — the answer is the min cost to get past the last step.

name: Min Cost to Connect All Points
hints: You want the cheapest set of edges connecting all points — that's a Minimum Spanning Tree.
Prim's algorithm grows the tree one cheapest available edge at a time from a min-heap.
Track visited points so you don't re-add edges to points already included in the tree.

name: Min Stack
hints: You need getMin() in O(1), so don't recompute it by scanning.
Store each pushed value together with the minimum of that value and the previous stack minimum. The first pair uses its own value as the minimum.
Popping removes both the value and its cached minimum, exposing the previous state's minimum. Duplicate minima are preserved naturally; getMin reads the top pair in O(1), with O(n) total storage.

name: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
hints: For each query, you want the smallest interval that contains it — process both in a smart order to avoid rechecking everything.
Sort both intervals and queries by value, and use a min-heap of active intervals keyed by interval size.
As you sweep through queries in increasing order, add newly-started intervals to the heap and pop expired ones off the top before reading the answer.

name: Minimum Platforms
hints: The answer is the maximum number of trains occupying platforms simultaneously, not the total number of arrivals.
Sort trains by arrival time while retaining their departure times. A min-heap of active departures lets you release finished trains before inserting the next one.

Track the largest heap size. For this platform problem, retain departures equal to the incoming arrival time; the same instant cannot serve both trains. A sorted arrival/departure sweep is an alternative.

name: Minimum Path Sum
hints: Similar shape to Unique Paths, but now summing costs instead of counting paths.
Each cell's min cost is its own value plus the smaller of the cell above or to the left.
The first row and first column can only be reached one way each, so they're computed as running sums.

name: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
hints: You want the shortest window whose sum is at least the target — classic shrinking window.
Expand the window right, and while the sum meets the target, shrink from the left and track the min length.
Every element is added once and removed at most once, keeping this O(n).

name: Minimum Window Substring
hints: Expand the window until it contains all required characters, then shrink from the left as much as possible.
Track how many required unique characters currently have their full count satisfied.
Only shrink while that satisfied count still equals the number of unique required characters.

name: Missing Number
hints: You know the full expected set (0 to n) — compare it against what's actually present.
The sum of 0 through n minus the sum of the given array leaves exactly the missing number.
XOR-ing every index 0 through n with every array value also isolates the missing number, avoiding any overflow concerns with large sums.

name: Multiply Strings
hints: You can't convert to native integers if the numbers can be arbitrarily large.
Multiply digit by digit like grade-school long multiplication, placing each partial product at the right offset in a result array.
Digit i of the first number times digit j of the second number always lands at result positions i+j and i+j+1 — accumulate there and handle carries at the end.

name: N-Queens
hints: Place one queen per row, and only need to check that column, diagonal, and anti-diagonal are free.
Track used columns and both diagonal directions with sets for O(1) conflict checks.
A cell's two diagonals can be identified by (row - col) and (row + col), which stay constant along each diagonal.

name: Network Delay Time
hints: You want the shortest time for a signal to reach every node — single-source shortest path.
Dijkstra's algorithm, using a min-heap keyed by current best travel time, fits directly.
The answer is the max travel time across all nodes — if any node's unreached, return -1.

name: Geek's Training
hints: Today's choice depends on which activity was performed yesterday, not the full history of earlier activities.
For each day and chosen activity, add its points to the best previous-day total among the other two activities.
Initialize the three first-day totals directly and compute a fresh three-value row for each following day. Do not overwrite values still needed by another activity's transition.

name: Non-overlapping Intervals
hints: Think in reverse: instead of counting removals, maximize how many intervals you can keep.
Sort by end time, and greedily keep an interval whenever it starts at or after the last kept interval's end.
Sorting by end time (not start time) is the key detail — it's what makes the greedy choice provably optimal.

name: Number of 1 Bits
hints: You want to count set bits, which you can do by repeatedly isolating the lowest set bit.
n AND (n-1) clears the lowest set bit of n — count how many times you can do that before n becomes 0.
This runs in time proportional to the number of set bits, not the total bit width.

name: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
hints: Each group of mutually reachable nodes counts as one component.
Union-Find (or repeated DFS from unvisited nodes) groups nodes into components efficiently.
With Union-Find, the number of distinct roots left after processing every edge is your answer.

name: Number of Islands
hints: Each unvisited land cell you find is the start of a new island.
DFS or BFS from that cell, marking every connected land cell as visited, "sinks" the whole island at once.
Count how many times you start a fresh DFS/BFS from an unvisited land cell — that count is your answer.

name: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
hints: Checking every cell's path to both oceans directly is expensive — try working backward from the oceans instead.
DFS inland from every Pacific-bordering cell, and separately from every Atlantic-bordering cell, moving only to equal-or-higher neighbors.
A cell that got reached from both searches can flow to both oceans — that's your answer set.

name: Palindrome Linked List
hints: You want O(1) space, so copying to an array isn't the intended solution.
Find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then compare both halves.
Optionally restore the list's original structure afterward by reversing the second half back.

name: Palindrome Partitioning
hints: You want every way to cut the string such that each piece is a palindrome.
At each position, try every possible next cut, but only recurse into cuts that form a palindrome.
Precomputing which substrings are palindromes avoids re-checking the same substring repeatedly.

name: Palindromic Substrings
hints: Same expand-around-center idea as Longest Palindromic Substring, but now you count every valid expansion instead of tracking just the longest.
Every successful expansion step (even a length-1 or length-2 one) counts as one palindrome.
Total count equals the sum, over all centers, of how far each one successfully expands.

name: Partition Equal Subset Sum
hints: If the total sum is odd, it's immediately impossible to split evenly.
This reduces to "can some subset sum to exactly half the total" — classic 0/1 knapsack.
Track which sums are reachable using a boolean array, updating it in reverse to avoid reusing an item twice.

name: Partition Labels
hints: A letter's partition must extend at least to that letter's last occurrence anywhere in the string.
Precompute the last index of every character first.
Extend the current partition's boundary to the max last-occurrence of every character seen so far in it; close the partition when you reach that boundary.

name: Path Sum
hints: You're looking for any single root-to-leaf path summing to the target.
Recurse down, subtracting the current node's value from the remaining target.
Only check for a match at leaf nodes (no children) — an internal node with the right sum but children isn't a valid path.

name: Perfect Squares
hints: For every number n, you want the minimum count of perfect squares summing to it.
minCount(n) = 1 + min over every perfect square s ≤ n of minCount(n - s).
Build this bottom-up from 0 to n, reusing already-computed smaller answers.

name: Permutation in String
hints: A permutation match means the window's character counts exactly equal the target's.
Use a fixed-size window (length of s1) and compare frequency counts as it slides.
Track a single "matches" counter instead of comparing full frequency arrays every slide, for O(n).

name: Permutations
hints: Order matters here, unlike Subsets — every arrangement counts as distinct.
Track which elements are already used in the current path, and try every unused one at each position.
Swapping elements in place is a memory-efficient alternative to a separate used-tracking array.

name: Plus One
hints: Adding one only cascades into a carry when a digit is 9.
Starting from the last digit, if it's less than 9, just increment it and you're done immediately.
If every digit was a 9 (all become 0), you need one extra leading 1 digit at the front.

name: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node
hints: You want O(1) extra space, so a queue-based BFS isn't the intended solution for the perfect-tree version.
Use the next pointers already set on the current level to traverse it, while linking up the next level below.
A dummy head per level makes tracking "where to attach the next node" cleaner.

name: Pow(x, n)
hints: Multiplying x by itself n times is O(n) — you can do better by repeatedly squaring.
x^n equals (x^(n/2))^2 when n is even, and x times (x^(n/2))^2 when n is odd (using integer division).
A negative n just means computing the positive-power result and then taking its reciprocal.
A spanning tree connects every vertex with minimum total edge weight. This differs from minimizing each vertex's distance from a particular source.
Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from the current tree to an unvisited vertex. Skip heap entries whose destination is already included and accumulate each accepted edge once.

As an alternative, Kruskal sorts all edges and uses disjoint-set union to reject cycle-forming edges. For a connected graph, stop after accepting vertexCount - 1 edges; verify connectivity rather than assuming a partial forest is a tree.
name: Minimum Spanning Tree
Product of Array Except Self
hints: You can't use division if a zero is present, so think prefix and suffix products.
Build a prefix-product array from the left, then fold in a suffix product from the right.
You can do the suffix pass in-place on the output array, using one running variable instead of a second array.

name: Reconstruct Itinerary
hints: You need to use every ticket exactly once, in an order that's lexicographically smallest when multiple valid itineraries exist.
This is really an Eulerian path — visit neighbors in sorted order, but only finalize a stop after exhausting its options.
Build the route by appending nodes in a post-order DFS fashion, then reverse the result at the end.

name: Redundant Connection
hints: You're looking for the one edge that turns a tree into a graph with a cycle.
Union-Find lets you add edges one at a time and detect the instant one connects two already-connected nodes.
That first edge connecting an already-unified pair is your answer — no need to look further.

name: Regular Expression Matching
hints: A star means zero-or-more of the preceding character, which forces you to consider two branches at once.
dp[i][j] represents whether the first i characters of s match the first j characters of the pattern.
On a star, you must handle both "match zero of the preceding char" and "match one more and stay on this pattern position."

name: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
hints: The array is sorted, so duplicates are always adjacent.
Use a slow pointer for the next unique-write position and a fast pointer to scan.
Only advance the slow pointer (and write) when the fast pointer finds a new value.

name: Remove Element
hints: You need to remove all instances of a value in place, order doesn't matter.
Use a slow pointer marking the next valid write position.
Only copy and advance the slow pointer when the current element isn't the target value.

name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
hints: You want to avoid two full passes (one to count, one to remove).
Move one pointer n steps ahead first, then move both pointers together until the lead reaches the end.
Use a dummy node before the head so removing the actual head node needs no special case.

name: Reorder List
hints: The target order interleaves the first half with the reversed second half.
Find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately.
Be careful to cleanly split the list in two and null-terminate the first half before reversing the second.

name: Reverse Bits
hints: You're reversing the order of all 32 bits, not the value itself.
Build the result bit by bit: shift the result left, then OR in the current lowest bit of the input.
Shift the input right by 1 each iteration so its next lowest bit is ready to read, across all 32 iterations.

name: Reverse Integer
hints: You need to catch 32-bit signed integer overflow, which reversing digits can easily cause.
Pull off the last digit with modulo 10, build the reversed number with result = result*10 + digit, and strip that digit off the original by dividing by 10.
Check for overflow before each multiply-by-10 step, comparing against the 32-bit int boundaries rather than after the fact.

name: Reverse Linked List
hints: You need to flip every next pointer — track the previous node as you go.
At each node, save its next before overwriting it, then point back to the previous node.
Also solvable recursively: reverse the rest of the list first, then fix the current node's links.

name: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
hints: You're reversing the list in fixed-size chunks — check if a full group of k even exists first.
Reverse each group of k like a standard linked-list reversal, tracking the group's original head and tail.
Connect the previous group's tail to the new group's head, and leave any remaining shorter group unreversed.

name: Roman to Integer
hints: Most symbols just add their value, but a smaller value before a larger one means subtract.
Scan left to right, and if the current symbol's value is less than the next symbol's, subtract it instead of adding.
A single pass with a value lookup map handles every case, including subtractive pairs like IV and IX.

name: Rotate Array
hints: Rotating in place with O(1) extra space is possible via three reversals.
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the rest.
Those three reversals together produce exactly a right-rotation by k.

name: Rotate Image
hints: You must rotate the matrix in place, without allocating a second matrix.
Transpose the matrix first (swap across the diagonal), then reverse each row.
Transpose plus reverse-rows together produce exactly a 90-degree clockwise rotation.

name: Rotate List
hints: Rotating by k is easier if you first connect the list into a circle.
Find the length, connect tail to head, then break the circle at the new correct point.
Take k modulo length first — rotating by the full length (or a multiple) is a no-op.

name: Rotting Oranges
hints: All oranges rot simultaneously each minute, which points to a multi-source BFS, not one BFS per rotten orange.
Push every initially-rotten orange into the queue at once, then process level by level, one minute per level.
If any fresh orange remains unreached after the BFS finishes, the answer is -1.

name: Same Tree
hints: Two trees are the same only if every corresponding node matches, including null positions.
If both nodes are null, that's a match; if only one is null, that's a mismatch.
Otherwise compare values, then recursively check the left and right subtrees.

name: Search a 2D Matrix
hints: Rows are sorted and each row's first element is greater than the previous row's last — think of it as one flattened sorted array.
Convert a single mid index into (row, col) using division and modulo by the row width.
Binary search that flattened index space directly instead of searching rows then columns separately.

name: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
hints: At every step, at least one half of the current range is normally sorted.
Figure out which half is sorted first, then check if the target falls in that half's range.
If the target's in the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.

name: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
hints: You need a format that unambiguously marks null children so deserialization isn't guesswork.
A preorder traversal that explicitly writes a marker (like N) for every null child works well.
Deserialize by consuming that same preorder stream recursively, exactly mirroring how you wrote it.

name: Set Matrix Zeroes
hints: You need O(1) extra space, so a separate copy of the matrix isn't the intended solution.
Use the matrix's own first row and first column as markers for which rows/columns need zeroing.
Handle the first row and first column's own zero-status with one or two separate boolean flags, since they double as your marker space.

name: Simplify Path
hints: Split the path on "/" and process each segment as a stack operation.
"." means stay, ".." means pop (go up a directory), anything else pushes a new directory name.
Join the remaining stack contents with "/" at the end, handling the root-only edge case.

name: Single Number
hints: Every number except one appears exactly twice — think about an operation where duplicates cancel out.
XOR-ing a number with itself gives 0, and XOR-ing with 0 leaves a number unchanged.
XOR every element together — every pair of duplicates cancels, leaving only the single number.

name: Sliding Window Maximum
hints: A brute-force max per window is O(n*k) — a monotonic deque gets you O(n).
Keep indices in a deque where corresponding values are in decreasing order.
Pop smaller values off the back before pushing, and pop the front once it slides out of the window.

name: Snakes and Ladders
hints: This is shortest-path (BFS) over board squares 1 to n², where snakes/ladders are just extra edges.
Convert the boustrophedon (back-and-forth) row layout into a straight-line square number to simplify indexing.
From a square, try every dice roll 1-6, following a snake/ladder immediately if the destination has one.

name: Spiral Matrix
hints: Track four shrinking boundaries — top, bottom, left, right — and walk each edge in turn.
Traverse right along the top boundary, down the right boundary, left along the bottom, up along the left, then shrink all four boundaries inward.
After each direction, re-check that top is at or above bottom and left is at or before right before continuing, since a non-square matrix can finish mid-cycle.

name: Can you answer these queries I
Sqrt(x)
hints: You want the floor of the square root without using a library function.
Binary search over possible answers from 0 to x, checking if mid*mid overshoots x.
Watch for overflow when squaring mid on very large inputs — use a wider integer type or divide instead of multiply.

name: String to Integer (atoi)
hints: This is mostly about carefully handling edge cases, not a clever algorithm.
Skip leading whitespace, then an optional sign, then digits — stop at the first non-digit.
Clamp the final result to the 32-bit signed integer range rather than overflowing.

name: Subset Sum Problem
hints: For each value, either use it once or skip it. Record whether each exact sum is reachable rather than storing every chosen subset.
Initialize only sum zero as reachable. For a one-dimensional table, visit sums downward when processing a value so it cannot be counted twice.
A value larger than the target can be skipped for nonnegative inputs. Zero does not change boolean reachability, though it matters when a later variant asks for the number of subsets.

name: Subsets
hints: Every element has two choices at each step: include it, or don't.
A recursive function that branches on include vs skip for each index generates all subsets.
There's no need to check for duplicates here — all elements are distinct, so no extra pruning is required.

name: Subsets II
hints: Duplicate values in the input mean naive subset generation will produce duplicate subsets.
Sort the array first so duplicates sit next to each other.
At each recursion level, skip a candidate if it equals the previous one and the previous one wasn't included at this same level.

name: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
hints: All words are the same length, so valid substrings align on fixed-size word boundaries.
Slide a window of total-words-length, breaking it into word-sized chunks and counting them.
Compare that window's word-count map against the target word-count map for an exact match.

name: Subtree of Another Tree
hints: You can reuse a "same tree" check as a helper here.
Walk every node in the main tree, and at each one check if that same-tree comparison matches the subtree.
Try the match starting at every node, not just the root — the subtree could start anywhere.

name: Sudoku Solver
hints: This is backtracking over empty cells, trying digits 1-9 and checking row/column/box validity.
Track used digits per row, column, and 3x3 box (similar to Valid Sudoku) for O(1) conflict checks.
On placing a digit that leads to a dead end, undo it (backtrack) and try the next digit before giving up on the cell.

name: Sum of Two Integers
hints: You can't use plus or minus directly, so build addition from bitwise operations instead.
XOR gives you the sum of two bits ignoring carry; AND, shifted left by 1, gives you the carry.
Repeat that XOR/AND-shift process, feeding the carry back in, until there's no carry left to add.

name: Surrounded Regions
hints: An O region is only safe if it touches the border somewhere.
Start DFS/BFS from every border O first, and mark everything reachable from those as safe.
Afterward, flip every remaining unmarked O to X — those never had a path to the border.

name: Swap Nodes in Pairs
hints: You're relinking pointers two nodes at a time, not swapping values.
Use a dummy node before the head so the first pair swap has no special case.
At each step, rewire prev/first/second's next pointers in the right order before advancing.

name: Swim in Rising Water
hints: You want the path where the single highest elevation crossed is as small as possible.
A modified Dijkstra works: instead of summing distances, track the max elevation seen so far on each path.
A min-heap ordered by that running max, always expanding the currently-lowest-max cell, gets you there efficiently.

name: Symmetric Tree
hints: A tree is symmetric if its left subtree is a mirror image of its right subtree.
Write a helper comparing two subtrees where you check node1.left against node2.right, and node1.right against node2.left.
Both null is a match; only one null, or mismatched values, is not.

name: Target Sum
hints: Assigning plus or minus to each number is really choosing a subset to negate.
If S is the total sum and P is the positive-subset sum, the negative subset sums to S-P, and you need P - (S-P) to equal target.
That reframes it as: count subsets summing to (target + S) / 2 — a counting variant of the subset-sum knapsack.

name: Task Scheduler
hints: Among tasks currently allowed to run, prefer the one with the most remaining occurrences. A max-heap can maintain that priority.
After running a task at time t, enqueue its remaining count with release time t + cooldown + 1. Before choosing the next task, return every released entry to the heap.

If the ready heap is empty, jump to the earliest cooldown release instead of simulating every idle slot. Stop only when both structures are empty; with time starting at zero, the schedule length is the last occupied time plus one.

name: Time Based Key-Value Store
hints: Each key maps to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs, added in increasing timestamp order.
That means each key's list is already sorted by timestamp — binary search applies.
Find the largest timestamp in that key's list that is at most the query timestamp.

name: Top K Frequent Elements
hints: First count how often each element appears.
Keep a min-heap of at most k (frequency, value) pairs. Removing the smallest pair discards the weakest retained candidate.

GFG breaks equal-frequency ties in favor of the larger value and requires descending priority order. Extract the retained pairs and reverse that order; LeetCode accepts any order for its selected values.

name: Top K Frequent Words
hints: Ties in frequency break by lexicographic order, which affects both counting and comparison.
Count word frequencies first, then use a heap ordered by (frequency, word) with a custom comparator.
A min-heap of size k (popping the worst candidate when it overflows) avoids sorting the entire word list.

name: Trapping Rain Water
hints: Water needs two walls taller than a valley floor. A decreasing stack can retain unresolved walls until a taller right wall arrives.
Store indices. While the current height exceeds the stack top's height, pop that valley floor. If the stack becomes empty, there is no left wall for this layer.
Otherwise, the new top is the left wall. Add (currentIndex - leftIndex - 1) * (min(leftHeight, currentHeight) - floorHeight), then continue popping. Each pop accounts for one newly bounded layer.

name: Triangle
